exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient on ART presents with fever and purulent wound drainage – what is your next step? — Obtain wound culture, start empiric anti‑pseudomonal therapy, and assess for sepsis.
Why would you choose cefepime over ceftriaxone for a ventilated patient with new infiltrates? — Cefepime covers Pseudomonas, whereas ceftriaxone does not.
A patient on meropenem develops rising creatinine – how do you modify therapy? — Switch to a non‑nephrotoxic anti‑pseudomonal β‑lactam (e.g., ceftazidime) and monitor renal function.

Explain how you would differentiate Pseudomonas pneumonia from malaria‑related pulmonary edema in a low‑resource setting. — Look for productive purulent sputum, Gram‑negative rods on smear, and recent antibiotic exposure; malaria shows haemolysis, cyclic fever, and peripheral smear parasites.
What is the role of combination therapy (β‑lactam + aminoglycoside) in severe Pseudomonas sepsis? — Provides synergistic killing and reduces resistance emergence; use only if renal function allows.
When is it appropriate to de‑escalate from broad‑spectrum to narrow‑spectrum antibiotics? — After culture results show susceptibility to a narrower agent and the patient is clinically stable.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with fever and urinary symptoms – why consider Pseudomonas? — Sickle‑cell patients often have indwelling catheters and are immunocompromised, increasing risk for Gram‑negative UTI.
What warning signs indicate the need for urgent ICU transfer in Pseudomonas sepsis? — Hypotension refractory to fluids, altered mental status, respiratory failure, oliguria, or rising lactate.
ai.title: Management of Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infections
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes severe infections in low‑resource settings, especially in immunocompromised patients. Recognise risk factors, use appropriate diagnostics, and choose effective antibiotics while considering local resistance patterns.

b: Common in ICU, burns, catheterised patients
High mortality if untreated or resistant
sections.p: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic Gram‑negative bacillus that thrives in moist environments and hospital equipment. It causes pneumonia, urinary‑tract infection, wound infection, septicemia and otitis, often in patients with HIV, TB, malaria, sickle‑cell disease or after broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

b: Risk factors: recent antibiotics, neutropaenia, ventilator, dialysis
Typical presentation: fever, purulent discharge, worsening organ dysfunction
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion plus culture from a sterile site. Resistance mechanisms include β‑lactamases, efflux pumps and porin loss. Empiric therapy must cover likely resistant strains until sensitivities return.

t.a: Blood, urine, sputum or wound culture
t.b: Identifies organism and susceptibility – guides definitive therapy
Rapid clue – Gram‑negative rods with polar flagella suggest Pseudomonas
Detects organ failure that may dictate urgency of treatment

b: Empiric choice must consider local resistance rates
Early appropriate therapy reduces mortality by up to 30 %
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, lack of advanced microbiology may force clinicians to rely on syndromic treatment. Knowing local antibiograms and the most effective empiric agents (e.g., ceftazidime, cefepime, piperacillin‑tazobactam, carbapenems) is essential.
